blocks.content: You open a file to fix one tiny bug. Two hours later you are still reading it, and somehow you have touched six other things you never meant to.
That feeling has a name. It is the feeling of code that violates SOLID.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782846003677-24760697.png
blocks.alt: From messy code to maintainable code through SOLID

blocks.content: SOLID is not about memorising five letters. It is about learning to recognise the smell of code that fights back every time you try to change it.

In this lesson we walk through all five principles, but from the other side. Instead of the rule, we look at the violation: what broken code actually looks like, why it hurts, and the smell that gives it away.
1. Violating SRP: the class that does everything
blocks.text: 1. Violating SRP: the class that does everything

blocks.content: The Single Responsibility Principle says a class should have one reason to change. The most common violation is the God Class, a single object that quietly collects unrelated jobs until nobody dares to touch it.
At first glance it feels convenient. Everything about an order lives in one place. But look at what this class actually owns:
["Business validation rules","Database persistence and raw SQL","Email formatting and delivery","PDF invoice layout and generation"]

Four completely unrelated reasons to change now live in one method. A change to your email template forces you to reopen the same file that holds your tax and SQL logic. One mistake there can break billing.
The smell

You try to describe the class and you need the word and. "It validates the order and saves it and emails the customer and builds the invoice." Every and is a hidden responsibility waiting to bite you.
2. Violating OCP: the switch that never stops growing
blocks.text: 2. Violating OCP: the switch that never stops growing

blocks.content: The Open Closed Principle says code should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new behaviour without editing code that already works. The classic violation is a long chain of if else or a switch that you must reopen for every new case.
Every new payment type means editing this exact method. Each edit risks breaking the cases that already shipped and were already tested. The blast radius of a new feature is the entire class.
The smell
Adding a feature means changing old code instead of adding new code. When you find yourself typing else if for the tenth time, OCP is being violated.
3. Violating LSP: the subclass that breaks the promise
blocks.text: 3. Violating LSP: the subclass that breaks the promise

blocks.content: The Liskov Substitution Principle says a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent is expected, without surprises. The violation is a child that cannot honour the contract its parent advertises.
On paper an Ostrich is a Bird, so inheritance feels right. But now any code that trusts the parent breaks:

The caller did everything correctly. It was promised a Bird that can fly, and the subclass quietly broke that promise. The bug shows up far away from the Ostrich class, which makes it painful to trace.
The smell

A subclass throws UnsupportedOperationException, returns null where the parent never would, or leaves an inherited method empty. If a child has to disable part of its parent, the inheritance is wrong.
4. Violating ISP: the fat interface
The Interface Segregation Principle says no class should be forced to depend on methods it does not use. The violation is one bloated interface that lumps unrelated capabilities together.

The OldPrinter only prints, but the Machine interface forces it to pretend it can scan and fax. It is dragged into changes it has nothing to do with. The day someone adds a staple method to the interface, every printer in the codebase stops compiling.
The smell
A class implements an interface but fills half the methods with empty bodies or exceptions. The interface is asking for more than any single client actually needs.
5. Violating DIP: welded to the details
blocks.text: 5. Violating DIP: welded to the details

blocks.content: The Dependency Inversion Principle says high level code should depend on abstractions, not on concrete details. The violation is a high level class that reaches out and builds its own low level dependency with new.
OrderService is now welded to MySQL. The consequences pile up:

["You cannot swap MySQL for Postgres without editing OrderService.","You cannot unit test placing an order without a real database running.","High level policy and low level storage are stuck in the same blob of code."]
items: You cannot swap MySQL for Postgres without editing OrderService.
You cannot unit test placing an order without a real database running.
High level policy and low level storage are stuck in the same blob of code.

blocks.content: The smell
A business class uses new to create a database, an email client, or an API client directly. The important code knows the brand name of its tools instead of just their job.
6. A quick smell checklist
You do not need to memorise five definitions. When something feels off, run through these questions:

["SRP: do I need the word \"and\" to describe this class?","OCP: to add a feature, am I editing old code instead of adding new code?","LSP: does any subclass throw, return null, or do nothing where the parent would not?","ISP: is a class forced to implement methods it leaves empty?","DIP: does my important logic build its own tools with \"new\"?"]
items: SRP: do I need the word "and" to describe this class?
OCP: to add a feature, am I editing old code instead of adding new code?
LSP: does any subclass throw, return null, or do nothing where the parent would not?
ISP: is a class forced to implement methods it leaves empty?
DIP: does my important logic build its own tools with "new"?

blocks.content: A violation is rarely one big mistake. It is a small shortcut that nobody cleaned up, repeated until the code became hard to change.
7. Common questions

Is every God Class a violation? - Almost always, yes, once it grows. A tiny script can hold a few jobs and stay readable. But the moment unrelated reasons to change share a file, SRP is already cracking. Watch the trend, not just the snapshot.

Is one if else statement an OCP violation? - No. A single branch is fine. The violation is the pattern: a growing chain that you must reopen for every new type. If new cases keep arriving, that is your signal to switch to extension.

How do I spot an LSP violation early? - Read the subclass and ask: does it weaken any promise the parent made? A narrower return, a new exception, or a stricter input are all red flags. If a subclass surprises a caller, it is breaking substitution.

Do these violations always need fixing right now? - No. A violation is a cost, not a crime. If the code is stable and rarely touched, leave it. Fix violations in the places that change often, because that is where they actually hurt you.

Spotting violations is the first half of the skill. Once you can name the smell, the next step is turning that messy code into something clean, one safe move at a time. That is exactly what we do in Refactoring to SOLID.
